newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS-Venezuela privatization program in disarray.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Venezuela privatization program in disarray.

text.p: Venezuela's decision to postpone the auction of Banco de Venezuela Wednesday has thrown the government's privatization program into disarray and reopened questions about its commitment to the sale of state assets.
"It looks bad because the sale was seen as a key part of the privatization program," said Simon Brad of the Banesco brokerage.

Esther de Margulis, president of the state's Deposits Guarantee Fund, known as FOGADE, announced Wednesday that the auction of Banco de Venezuela had been called off indefinitely because of confusion about the auction process.
"Due to these conditions FOGADE thinks it will be impossible to carry out a successful auction and has decided to suspend the auction process," she said at a news conference.

The sale of the bank, valued at a minimum price of $275 million, was thrown off course late last week when a local judge ordered the auction suspended while alleged irregularities were being investigated.
The same judge reversed her decision Monday after receiving more information from FOGADE, but the confusion shook the confidence of prospective bidders.

FOGADE sources told Reuters after the announcement Wednesday that only Banco Santander had remained interested in buying the bank. Peru's Banco de Credito, Colombia's Banco Bogota and Germany's Dresdner Bank AG had cooled on the idea.
The cancellation of the Banco de Venezuela sale capped a bad week for Venezuela's struggling privatization program.
FOGADE announced Tuesday that it had postponed the sale of Alucasa, a small aluminum concern, due to take place Friday. to give potential bidders more time to assess the company.

A base price of $45 million had been set for the company, which has an annual production capacity of 20,000 tonnes a year. It is 49 percent-owned by state-owned aluminum smelter Alcasa and 51 percent-owned by a group of private investors and banks, some of which are in turn owned by FOGADE.
Also on Tuesday, lawyers acting for Britain's World Aviation Group said the company had dropped out of the auction for Aeropostal, the bankrupt state airline.
Aeropostal is scheduled to be auctioned on Friday, marking the fourth attempt to sell the carrier since July 1994 in what has become a fitting emblem of Venezuela's privatization program.
After a promising start in 1991, Venezuela's initiative to sell state assets has virtually ground to a halt.
Since the government launched an International Monetary Fund-backed economic reform program on April 15, there have been high hopes that the drive would regain momentum.
Still, major sell-offs, such as the government's 49 percent stake in telephone company CANTV and four aluminum companies, have been slated for the end of the year.

The aluminum sector's privatization remained in doubt Wednesday after reports that government officials had failed to reach a deal with minority Japanese shareholders to relinquish their veto power in smelter Venalum.
And the failure to sell Banco de Venezuela will undoubtedly take much of the steam out of the government's recent progress.
"This is a major blow...Things were looking good until just recently," said one New York-based analyst.
